newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Narayanan rises from poverty to presidency.
newsitem.headline: India's Narayanan rises from poverty to presidency.

text.p: Kocheril Raman Narayanan, elected India's first low-caste president on Thursday, has defied social discrimination and risen from dire poverty to hold an array of prestige jobs.
On the long road to the British-built presidential palace on New Delhi's Raisina Hill, the 76-year-old leader has been a scholar, journalist, diplomat and government minister.
Left-leaning Narayanan, known for his tact learned from his days as a poor child, will take over as the head of state from Shankar Dayal Sharma, whose five-year term ends on July 25.
One of the five children of a practitioner of traditional Indian medicine, Narayanan belongs to the Dalit community, representing the lowest rung in the Hindu social hierarchy.

In his school days, Narayanan, who later studied at the London School of Economics, had to walk 10 miles (16 km) to school and faced the insult of being turned out of a classroom once because he could not pay his fees.
"Those bitter experiences taught me forebearance and diplomacy," he said in a recent interview.
Parties of all hues backed him in the presidential race in a phase of coalition politics where the job of a traditional figurehead has become crucial in forming governments.
Narayanan started his career as a journalist and worked in two English-language newspapers, The Hindu in Madras and Times of India in Bombay, before resuming studies in London.
With a recommendation from his socialist mentor in London, Harold Laski, Narayanan befriended India's first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, and remained close to his powerful family.

Narayanan joined the Indian Foreign Service in 1949 to begin a 35-year career as a diplomat. On his first posting to Rangoon, he met his future wife, Burmese university teacher Tint Tint, who later took an Indian name, Usha. They have two daughters.
Narayanan has served as India's envoy in Turkey, China, Thailand and the United States.
In 1984, he became a lawmaker for the Congress party and served as junior minister for planning and later, foreign affairs. He won parliamentary re-election in 1984 and 1991.
In 1992, Narayanan was elected vice president of India. His subsequent ascent coincided with the rise of low-caste parties.

Though raised in poverty, Narayanan is known have richer tastes. "Narayanan has simplicity but he is not a Gandhian," a nephew, Anirudhan, was quoted as saying in a reference to India's austere independence leader, Mahatma Gandhi.
